question: In 2021, a group of UN Special Rapporteurs and human rights experts issued a joint correspondence to the Chinese Government1 regarding credible allegations of forced organ harvesting in China.

The following year, Parliament adopted a resolution2 also raising concern over forced organ harvesting in China and called on ‘the relevant institutions in the Member States to evaluate and revisit the terms of their collaborations with Chinese institutions on transplant medicine, research and training’.

This, coupled with the launch of ‘New Horizon’ – an EU-China transplant training programme, whose honoured guest, Professor Shusen Zheng, is a Chinese transplant surgeon accused of involvement in forced organ harvesting3 – has raised concerns over whether this allocation of funding upholds EU values.
Given that EU funds may have unintentionally supported forced organ harvesting, we would like to kindly ask the Commission: 1.
What mechanisms are in place to prevent EU complicity in forced organ harvesting when funding medical collaborations involving non-EU countries?
Will the Commission investigate any EU-funded medical programmes which may be aiding and abetting forced organ harvesting?

China: UN human rights experts alarmed by ‘organ harvesting’ allegations | OHCHR https://spcommreports.ohchr.org/TMResultsBase/DownLoadPublicCommunicationFile?gId=26382. Texts adopted, P9_TA(2022)0200, ‘Reports of continued organ harvesting in China’ Thursday, 5 May 2022 (europa.eu). Oxford University held training sessions for Chinese doctors accused of harvesting organs (telegraph.co.uk).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.6.2024) 1. Legal entities from third countries are eligible to receive funding from the EU budget to which the associated third country is obliged to pay a financial contribution, which constitutes an external assigned revenue of the EU budget.

The EU-funded research must comply with ethical principles and relevant European, national and international legislation including the EU’s Charter of Fundamental Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights and its Supplementary Protocols1. All proposals addressing human health are subject to an ethics screening.

If serious and/or complex ethics issues are identified, a specific ethical evaluation is performed. This is obligatory when the research involves human participants, their cells or tissues, or when research is conducted outside the EU. Compliance with ethical standards is also provided for in the grant agreements2.

For the use of human cells or tissues, the beneficiaries are obliged to follow in particular: Directive 2004/23/EC on setting standards of quality and safety for the donation, procurement, testing, processing, preservation, storage and distribution of human tissues and cells3, and Council Directive 2010/45/EU on standards of quality and safety of human organs intended for transplantation4.

Further specific obligations5 are envisaged in the ethics appraisal process. 2. The Commission is neither aware nor involved in the programme mentioned by the Honourable Member. The mentioned programme does not receive funding from the European Commission.
